T2A01: 2 m repeater offset: plus or minus 600 kHz.
T2A02: The 2 m national FM simplex calling frequency is 146.520 MHz.
T2A03: 70 cm repeater offset: plus or minus 5 MHz.
T2A04: On a repeater: say their call sign, then yours. 'Break break' is for emergencies.
T2A05: Answering a CQ: their call first, then yours.
T2A06: Simplex phone CQ: 'CQ' a few times, 'this is', your call, then listen. Repeat as needed.
T2A07: Repeater offset = the difference between a repeater's transmit and receive frequencies.
T2A09: On a repeater, say your call sign and 'listening'. No CQ on repeaters.
T2A10: A band plan is a voluntary guideline for which modes and activities go where in a band.
T2A11: Simplex = transmitting and receiving on the same frequency.
T2B01: Reverse swaps your frequencies so you listen on the repeater's input. That tells you whether you could reach the other station on simplex.
T2B02: CTCSS is a sub-audible tone sent with your voice to open a repeater's squelch.
T2B03: Linked repeaters: whatever one receives, all of them transmit.
T2B04: If you can hear a repeater but can't get in: all of these are possible causes. Wrong offset, wrong CTCSS tone, or wrong DCS code.
T2B05: Audio dropping out on voice peaks on FM means you're talking too loudly (over-deviating).
T2B06: DTMF = two simultaneous tones (the telephone keypad).
T2B07: To join a DMR talkgroup, program its ID into your radio.
T2B08: If two stations interfere on the same frequency, they negotiate. Nobody owns a frequency.
T2B09: Simplex channels let nearby stations talk directly without tying up a repeater.
T2B10: QRM = interference from other stations (man-made). QRN = natural noise.
T2B12: DMR color code: an access code your radio must have to use a particular repeater.
T2B13: Squelch mutes the receiver when no signal is present.
T2B14: A DMR talkgroup organizes traffic so you only hear the group you want.
T2C01: FCC rules always apply, even during RACES, ARES, or FEMA operations.
T2C02: Net control calls the net to order and directs the stations checking in.
T2C03: Spell unusual words with a standard phonetic alphabet.
T2C04: RACES is the FCC Part 97 service for civil defense communications in national emergencies.
T2C05: Traffic = formal messages passed through a net.
T2C06: ARES: licensed hams who voluntarily register their skills and equipment for public service.
T2C07: In a net, transmit only when net control directs you, unless you're reporting an emergency.
T2C08: Winlink relays email using call-sign-based email addresses.
T2C09: You can go outside your privileges only when there's an immediate threat to life or property.
T2C10: A message preamble holds the information needed to track the message.
T2C11: The check in a radiogram is the word count of the message text.
T2C12: RACES requires certification by a civil defense agency. ARES doesn't.
T3A01: Moving a few feet changes how reflected copies of the signal combine (multipath), so they add or cancel.
T3A02: Leaves and branches absorb UHF and microwave signals.
T3A03: Long-distance VHF/UHF CW and SSB use horizontal polarization. FM and repeaters use vertical.
T3A04: Cross-polarized antennas (one vertical, one horizontal) mean much weaker signals.
T3A05: If buildings block the direct path, aim for a reflection that bounces your signal to the repeater.
T3A06: Picket fencing: rapid flutter on mobile signals as you drive through multipath.
T3A07: Rain and other precipitation absorb microwaves, cutting range.
T3A08: Irregular HF fading comes from copies of the signal arriving by different paths and combining randomly.
T3A09: Ionospheric signals come back elliptically polarized, so either vertical or horizontal antennas work.
T3A10: Multipath scrambles data, so error rates rise.
T3A12: Fog and rain have little effect on 10 m and 6 m. Weather only matters at microwave frequencies.
T3B01: A radio wave's electric and magnetic fields are at right angles to each other.
T3B02: Polarization = the orientation of the electric field.
T3B03: A radio wave has two components: electric and magnetic fields.
T3B04: Radio waves travel at the speed of light. They are light, at a lower frequency.
T3B06: Wavelength in meters = 300 / frequency in MHz. For example, 300 / 146 = about 2 m.
T3B07: Bands are also named by approximate wavelength: 2 meters, 70 centimeters.
T3B10: HF = 3-30 MHz. Each range is 10 times the one below: HF 3-30, VHF 30-300, UHF 300-3000 MHz.
T3B11: Speed of light: 300,000,000 meters per second.
T3B12: All radio frequencies travel at the same speed in free space.
T3C01: UHF passes right through the ionosphere instead of bouncing back, so it stops at the horizon.
T3C02: HF bounces off the ionosphere, so long-distance contacts are far more common on HF.
T3C03: Auroral signals sound distorted and raspy.
T3C04: Sudden strong signals beyond the horizon on 10, 6, and 2 m: sporadic E.
T3C05: Knife-edge diffraction bends signals over sharp obstructions like ridges.
T3C06: Regular over-the-horizon VHF/UHF out to about 300 miles: tropospheric ducting.
T3C07: Meteor scatter works best on 6 m.
T3C08: Tropospheric ducting is caused by temperature inversions.
T3C09: 10 m F-region DX: daytime (dawn to just after sunset), during high sunspot activity.
T3C10: At the sunspot peak, 6 and 10 m can open for F-region DX.
T3C11: The atmosphere bends radio waves slightly, so the radio horizon is a bit farther than the visual one.
T4A01: A 50 W mobile rig runs on 13.8 V and needs about 12 A when transmitting.
T4A02: Choose an SWR meter rated for the frequencies and power you'll use.
T4A03: Short, heavy DC power leads minimize voltage drop when the rig draws big current on transmit.
T4A04: FT8: the rig's audio connects to the audio input and output of a computer running FT8 software.
T4A05: An RF power meter goes in the feed line, between the transmitter and the antenna.
T4A06: A digital-mode interface carries receive audio, transmit audio, and transmitter keying (PTT).
T4A07: The computer's line-in connects to the transceiver's speaker output (receive audio into the computer).
T4A08: For RF bonding, use flat copper strap: low inductance.
T4A09: Battery run time = amp-hours / average current draw.
T4A10: A hotspot connects nearby radios to a digital voice or data network over the internet.
T4A11: A mobile rig's negative lead goes to the battery's chassis ground connection.
T4A12: An electronic keyer helps you send Morse code by hand (it makes the dits and dahs).
T4B01: Too much mic gain on SSB means distorted transmitted audio.
T4B02: Enter a frequency with the keypad or the VFO knob.
T4B03: To hear a weak FM signal, set the squelch so the audio stays open all the time.
T4B04: FM received slightly off frequency sounds distorted.
T4B05: Scanning tunes through frequencies looking for activity.
T4B06: SSB voice sounds too high or low? Adjust RIT (the clarifier). It shifts receive without changing transmit.
T4B07: A DMR code plug is the configuration file loaded into the radio: repeaters, talkgroups, and so on.
T4B08: Choosing a filter bandwidth that matches the mode cuts noise and interference.
T4B09: Select a DMR group by entering the group's ID code.
T4B10: SSB voice is about 2.4 kHz wide, so a 2400 Hz filter gives the best signal-to-noise.
T4B11: A D-STAR radio must have your call sign programmed in before you transmit.
